title: They shall keep it (Exodus 31:16–17)
hookLine: V'shamru is sung Friday night and Saturday morning
last: ALREADY ENOUGH, JUST AS IT IS.

cards: Some lines get stuck in a family. A grandparent's saying that comes out at every dinner. A song at every birthday.
Two verses from Exodus are like that for Shabbat. They're sung on Friday night, right before the evening Amidah. They're said again inside the Saturday morning Amidah in many communities.
And in many homes they open the Kiddush over wine at Saturday lunch. It's the kind of tune a child can hum before knowing what the words mean. It's called V'shamru, and they shall keep.

teach.b: Here they are in the old Jewish translation, from Exodus thirty-one: "Wherefore the children of Israel shall keep the sabbath, to observe the sabbath throughout their generations, for a perpetual covenant. It is a sign between Me and the children of Israel for ever."
Then the reason: because in six days God made heaven and earth, and on the seventh day ceased from work and rested. A few things are packed in there. First, keep.
Shamar in Hebrew means to guard, to watch over, the way you'd keep a garden or keep a secret. Shabbat isn't only something you have; it's something you protect.

Second, throughout their generations: not a one-time event, but a thing handed down, parent to child, like the tune. Third, a sign, like a family name over a door: a small, visible thing that says there's a bond here.
And then the last word of the passage, the one translated rested.
In Hebrew it's vayinafash, built from nefesh, soul, or breath. Some render it was refreshed, or caught breath. The Talmud plays with that word.
Resh Lakish taught that on Shabbat a person is given an extra soul, a neshamah yeteirah, and when Shabbat ends it's taken away.
He read vayinafash as a play on words: vay, avdah nefesh. Alas, the soul is lost. Some readers hear in it a reason Saturday night can feel a little sad: something extra was there, and now it's going.

how: V'shamru (Exodus 31:16–17) is sung in the Friday evening service before the Amidah in many communities, said in the Shabbat morning Amidah in the Ashkenazi rite, and recited at the start of the daytime Kiddush in many homes.

o: and they shall remember: the Ten Commandments
and they shall keep: verses on guarding the Sabbath
and they shall rest: a blessing over Sabbath candles

p: between God and Israel for ever

s: V'shamru is sung only once a week
Friday night, Saturday morning, and in many homes at the daytime Kiddush.
the Hebrew for keep also means to guard
shamar: to watch over, like a garden.
the Talmud speaks of an extra soul on Shabbat
given when Shabbat begins, taken when it ends.

games.q: the verse says God rested on the seventh day: vayinafash. how does one Talmud teacher read that word?
o: alas, the soul is lost: the extra Shabbat soul leaves at the end.
games.why: vay, avdah nefesh: the extra soul given on Shabbat is taken away when it ends.

practice: If you know the tune, sing v'shamru quietly; if not, sing the English, and they shall keep, to any slow melody, a few times over.
Then let the singing stop, think of one hour this week you'd like to guard, the way you'd guard a garden gate, and breathe into it.

wordCard.voice: V'shamru. And they shall keep: Exodus 31's words for the Sabbath, a sign for ever, guarded and handed down, sung all through the day.

orig.note: Hebrew: and they shall keep. the first word of Exodus 31:16.

carryVoice: Your line: keep the sabbath. To keep is to guard, and to hand it down. Six hundred eighteen days, done.
